#1437. Record-breaking Harry Kane belongs in the company of greats that he keeps. There is only one gap in his record now and he remains as central to ending 60 years of hurt than he has ever been, writes OLIVER HOLT

Published: 16:54 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 20:17 EST, 12 November 2026

Only giants have trodden the path that Harry Kane walked at Wembley on Thursday when he strode out on to the pitch on a bitterly cold winter night, his four young children by his side, and beheld the array of trophies, honours, adulation and respect that awaited him.

It is just 16 days since Kane held his hands to his face, climbed up to the stage at the London Palladium and said 'wow' when Ronaldo 'Il Fenomeno' presented him with the Ballon d'Or trophy that anointed him the best player in the world.

Now, it sat before him on a plinth and Kane broke away from the England line-up and walked forward to hoist it aloft. He showed it to all the corners of the stadium and for a moment, it was framed against the giant tifo bearing his image and the words 'England's Finest' that towered over one end of the ground.

But the Ballon d’Or is old news in the flood of honours that is coming Kane’s way in this golden summer of a great career. Kane had become the first Englishman to win the Ballon d’Or for a quarter of a century and on Thursday night he was to break the 37-year-old record held by Peter Shilton for the most England caps. He scored the winner, too. Of course, he did.

The occasion of England-Croatia in the Nations League was Kane's 126th appearance in an England shirt and Shilton stepped forward to hand him a small case containing a crest to mark the achievement. Finally, the Prince of Wales showed his appreciation to the England captain by presenting him with a commemorative shirt with 'Kane 126' emblazoned on it.

It was a night to feel the weight of football's history and the ghosts of greatness that people England's heritage. Kane belongs in the company he now keeps. He belongs in the pantheon of the game because he is one of the deadliest strikers in history. He belongs in the pantheon because of the humility he has shown and the dedication he devotes to improvement.

Harry Kane celebrated his record-breaking England appearance with a finely struck penalty

Before kick-off, Kane's history-making was celebrated with a commemorative shirt by the Prince of Wales

England (4-2-3-1): Pickford 6; Alexander-Arnold 6 (White 78, 6), Quansah 4, Burn 6, Hall 7; Rice 5 (Garner 78, 5), Anderson 6; Rogers 8, Bellingham 6, Gordon 5 (Ngumoha 78, 5); Kane 7

Croatia (4-2-3-1): Livakovic 5; Smolcic 6 (Marco Pasalic 76 5), Stanisic 6, Vuskovic 6, Gvardiol 5; Misic 5 (Modric 76, 6), Kovacic 6; Sucic 7 (Mario Pasalic 70, 5), Baturina 6, Vlasic 5; Matanovic 5 (Budimir 70, 5)

He belongs with Billy Wright, the first England player to 100 caps, and the man who set the England appearance record at 105 when he played for his country for the last time in 1959. He belongs with Bobby Charlton, who made it to 106 before the heartbreak of the 1970 World Cup quarter-final defeat to West Germany brought his international career to an end.

Kane belongs with Bobby Moore, Charlton's rival as the greatest England player of all time, who reached the new mark of 108 caps in November 1973. That was one of the great numbers in English sport until Peter Shilton finally surpassed it. He reached 125 caps by the time he played his last game for England in the third-place play-off at the 1990 World Cup.

It is quite some lineage. And now it is Kane who holds the prize. And if this was hardly a momentous match, it was a momentous occasion. If you are tired of glorying in a player like Kane, a relentless striker, a wonderful passer, the sweetest striker of the ball you will ever see, a player of vision, a man who exudes the beauty of simplicity and the wonder of modesty, then you are tired of football.

The honours are rushing at him in a giddy, babbling flood. It may be that he reaches close to 200 caps before he retires and even if it already seems likely that that record will be broken by Jude Bellingham, who has 61 caps at the age of 23, Kane's England goals tally, which stands at 92 after another goal against Croatia, will not be under threat for a generation or longer.

The gap, of course, is a tournament victory. That is what still separates Moore and Charlton from him. Kane is a dream of a player but he has not won the World Cup or the European Championship. What remains is the hope that he will put that right in the years that he has left in the game.

Winning the Nations League would not be quite the same but it would be a start and this victory over Croatia took England a small step closer to that goal. A convincing win over Spain in Madrid on Sunday would take them closer to their aim of finishing top of this group and getting a favourable draw in the quarter-finals in the spring.

Kane made his England debut in March 2015 when he was 21 and England's future looks brighter now than it did when he broke through. More than an hour before the game, the men who will follow Kane and perhaps even chase his caps record, chatted animatedly on the pitch. Bellingham, Morgan Rogers, Anthony Gordon and Morgan Gibbs-White are the new breed.

Morgan Rogers opened the scoring inside the opening half-an-hour and celebrated with his trademark cold celebration

England had found themselves pegged back by Croatia after slopping defending drew the visitors level

Referee Morten Krogh was summoned to the monitor to review the penalty shout on Thursday

Kane returned to Wembley triumphant for the first time since his historic Ballon d'Or win

After the Kane festivities, the first half was an anti-climax. Twenty-four minutes of relative drudgery ensued before Kane exhibited the breadth of his talent once again to help put England ahead. He got the ball 30 yards out, looked up and drifted a beautiful diagonal pass out to the right and into the path of Bellingham. Bellingham volleyed it across goal and Rogers forced it over the line.

The second half began slowly, too, but 15 minutes into it, Croatia equalised. England failed to clear a corner, Jarell Quansah tried to head the ball back to Jordan Pickford and, as Kane watched on, Petar Sucic stole in and hooked the ball past the England goalkeeper into the roof of the net.

Quansah made some kind of amends three minutes later when he was dragged down in the box and Danish referee Morten Krogh awarded a penalty. It was Kane-time again. Kane took the kick and lifted it gently and with a touch of curl down the centre of the goal. Dominic Livakovic dived to his left and the ball sailed softly over his trailing leg and into the net.

Croatia had chances to draw level but could not take them. England made changes and young Rio Ngumoha, a winger of rare talent, another with a rich future ahead of him, another who will help to fill the void when the day comes for Kane to bid farewell to England, came on as a late substitute for Gordon.

And so Kane's night of history began to draw to a close. In a 2-1 victory, he had made one and scored one. He remains as central to England's hopes of ending more than 60 years without a trophy as he ever has been. In a career that has festooned him with garlands and left no one in doubt of his greatness, it is the only gap that remains.

Harry Kane has set his sights firmly on rapidly reaching a century of international goals after becoming England’s most-capped player of all time.

The England skipper marked his 126th appearance for the Three Lions with the winner against Croatia in the Nations League – his first goal since picking up the Ballon d’Or last month.

Kane was afforded an emotional presentation pre-match at Wembley to mark both achievements and is already thinking of creating more history after moving within eight goals of a ton.

‘It’s achievable,’ Kane said. ‘I’m getting closer. Breaking the appearance record is a massive thing in the history of our game, seeing the tifo at the stadium and having my kids with me was beyond dreams.

‘It’s important to recognise our great players. It’s maybe something we haven’t done so well over the years with some of our other greats.

‘It's been a crazy few weeks. I don’t know if I’ve fully taken it all in. The reception has been overwhelming.

‘Maybe during the winter break I’ll be on a beach reflecting on everything I’ve achieved, having a drink with my wife.’

Croatia legend Luka Modric, 41, was part of the presentations ahead of kick off and Kane did not rule out attempting to prolong his career in a similar vein to the AC Milan midfielder.

‘He’s an inspiration for a lot of us,’ Kane added. ‘An incredible player and a great person, he’s looked after himself and still to be playing at this level is inspiring for me to push the limits. To see where your body and mentality takes you.

‘As long as I feel I can help, I’ll be here for as long as I can. If that’s until I’m 40, we’ll wait and see.’

Now qualified for the quarter-finals, England need to beat Spain in Madrid on Sunday to top their group and Thomas Tuchel believes they can topple the world champions.

‘It’s a completely different scenario, completely different setup,’ Tuchel said. ‘But I'm very positive that we will get what we want.’

#1435. Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews said. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

To play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

It was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak said. “I was waiting for my moment.”

Any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola said they will now be out “for some time”.

The loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

The injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa said: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”

To play this way requires quality when you do have the ball, and full-backs Keane Lewis-Potter and Michael Kayode deserve particular praise. They have contributed materially to Brentford’s attacks, helping their side to league-high successful crosses (26) and expected goals from set-pieces (4.03).

Manchester City’s claim to have “irrefutable evidence” that will overturn their guilty verdict on appeal is based on a trove of emails, letters and bank statements.

A re-examination of Abu Dhabi government documents, receipts and testimony from 24 witnesses – all of which the club believe were wrongly dismissed at the original hearing – will be central in attempts to force a full or partial acquittal or retrial, according to people familiar with the case.

City’s legal team will attempt to demonstrate “fundamental errors” in tests applied by an independent commission to the Premier League’s case that commercial revenue was artificially inflated by £920m. Sources with understanding of City’s case have told Telegraph Sport the club are bullish about their appeal, based on:

Shahid Khan, Fulham’s owner, insists that his team are on a “positive path” despite remaining winless in the Premier League after six matches.

In his programme notes, he wrote: “I want to reflect on our recent form. Prior to the international break, we were trending upward… That momentum carried us through most of Saturday’s match at Ipswich Town, but we all know how that ended. The result was devastating for all of us, and I won’t pretend otherwise.

“And yet, I am reminded of the positive path we have been on and the genuine potential of this team. Our squad is strong, while still coming together. We have been in every match, missing only the opportunities we’ve had to complete the task. I believe those opportunities will soon be seized.”

This feels like an extremely treacherous trip for Liverpool and for Andoni Iraola, who has a poor record against Brentford. With Bournemouth, he did not win any of his six matches against today’s opponents.

The good news for Liverpool is that Alexander Isak and Dominik Szoboszlai are fit enough to start the game, and that Brentford top scorer Kevin Schade is not. Schade is on the bench after picking up a shoulder injury against Aston Villa last weekend.

Barcola opened his Liverpool account on Wednesday and he will look to continue his goal-scoring form at the Gtech Community Stadium.

Speaking of the France winger, head coach Andoni Iraola said: “I think it’s still very early, especially for him who hasn’t played any minutes in pre-season, he’s kind of been doing pre-season in the first games with us almost [in] official games.

“It’s remarkable because to score three goals in a Champions League game is … not a lot of players can say they have done it.

“It’s something nice for him but I think the best thing is we can feel him, he seems with confidence on the ball [away] from the goals, straight away you could feel he was confident going in one-to-one situations, attacking the spaces and [those] are his strengths.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. It was exactly what the France winger needed, and with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo emerging as doubts for this afternoon’s trip to Brentford, the attacking burden may fall on Barcola and Florian Wirtz’s shoulders once more.

Breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be said for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Pressure was already mounting before Fulham’s three-game run against the promoted teams, and the late collapse at Portman Road will not have helped the Spaniard’s cause. Defeat by Hull City will not be seen kindly by the club’s hierarchy.

#1434. Bologna set on terminating Dovbyk’s loan

Artem Dovbyk, so far, hasn’t found the redemption he hoped for in Bologna.

The Ukrainian striker joined the Rossoblu on loan this summer with an option to buy, hoping to rediscover his best self. Nothing of the sort. The 1997-born striker has played just 105 minutes, scoring a goal against Sassuolo.

The Felsinei are far from satisfied with the former Girona player. Dovbyk hasn’t found any playing time under either Domenico Tedesco or Raffaele Palladino; the player isn’t convincing anyone at Bologna.

Bologna, as reported by Tuttosport, are dissatisfied with Artem Dovbyk’s performance, so much so that they’re considering terminating his loan six months early.

The Rossoblu club is already considering a replacement for the Ukrainian striker: Lorenzo Lucca, who is leaving Napoli.

The former Udinese player is a target for Palladino, who wants a striker more suited to his style of play than Dovbyk.

The situation will need to be monitored, pending concrete developments. Roma is aware that the 1997-born striker will have little room at Bologna.

#1432. Roma finalize permanent deal for Balerdi

Leonardo Balerdi has quickly become an important player for Gian Piero Gasperini.

Upon his arrival, the Grugliasco-born coach called him one of the new captains, given that he wore the captain’s armband at Marseille.

Born in 1999, the defender arrived on loan from OM, and the buyout is contingent on the defender’s appearances. To trigger the €11 million obligation, Balerdi will have to play 40% of the matches.

The figure increases if he makes more appearances: €14 million, with over 55% of matches lasting at least 45 minutes.

The former Marseille player could be satisfied with just 20% of the matches in the second half of the season. In this case, Roma would have to pay the French club €9 million.

Gasperini considers him an important player, and in a short time, he’s carved out a significant niche for himself, considering the starting lineup alongside Mancini, Ndicka, and Hermoso: 639 minutes, highlighted by a brace away to Napoli.

As La Gazzetta dello Sport reports, if an automatic buyout were to arrive, all the conditions are in place for this to happen: the Giallorossi club and the player are already in full agreement regarding the contract renewal. In fact, the parties have already put everything down in black and white. The desire of all is to continue together.

#1431. All hail James Trafford: How the most normal bloke in elite football became England’s No.1

James Trafford doesn’t immediately strike you as one of the world’s best goalkeepers.

You half-remember him from your student union days. Nice enough fella, just sort of there. Stoke City fan, you think. Went on to play guitar for a short-lived indie band that reached No.33 in the album charts.

Maybe that’s why he and Scott Parker didn’t immediately hit it off at Burnley. Trafford has described their “very, very weird start”, admitting that neither particularly liked the other and they struggled to connect.

No great surprise, really. Parker is very much a proper football man, the archetype of a limited but committed noughties English midfielder. The final boss of Tom Cleverleys. All the while Trafford is nobody’s idea of a typical footballer. He grew up riding tractors in Cumbria.

Yet here we are. Leeds United’s record signing, the most expensive English goalkeeper ever and the fourth-most expensive in history, is worth every penny. Of the 52 goalkeepers to have played at least 10 matches across Europe’s big five leagues this season, Trafford ranks first for save percentage, stopping an extraordinary 81.4% of shots he’s faced (credit to OPTA’s Jonny Cooper).

England Pod co-host George Elek took some serious pelters – mostly from Everton fans – for suggesting Trafford was already a better goalkeeper than the long-serving Jordan Pickford last summer.

“Didn’t realise so many people haven’t yet realised that Trafford is better than Pickford,” he posted.

“I’d say let’s come back to this in a year but it doesn’t look like Trafford’s going to play so you’ll just have to trust me I guess.”

Elek might yet have the last laugh. After all, covering the Football League is his day job, and he’d just witnessed Trafford produce one of the most remarkable individual campaigns in Championship history.

Under Parker, Burnley amassed 100 points, went 33 matches unbeaten and conceded just 16 goals in 46 games. Trafford played all but one of those matches, notching an off-the-scale 85.6% save percentage.

The Clarets were defensively well organised and would also miss CJ Egan-Riley after promotion, but their struggles in the top flight after Trafford returned to Manchester City exposed the limitations of Parker’s side. He had been covering for an awful lot.

Unfortunately, Trafford was unceremoniously shoved onto the bench after City swooped for the shiny new Gianluigi Donnarumma, fresh from his Champions League winning heroics at PSG.

Elek knew what Thomas Tuchel had on his hands, but had to bite his tongue as Trafford warmed the bench throughout City’s Premier League and Champions League campaigns.

He did get opportunities to impress in the domestic cups, which City went on to win, but the England manager was never realistically going to take a second-choice goalkeeper to the World Cup over a long-serving stalwart like Pickford.

Still, Tuchel might’ve been tempted by a goalkeeper who had delivered on some of the biggest occasions, as opposed to one who had spent the season watching from the sidelines. Trafford had tasted success at Wembley with City, whereas Pickford is the personification of that Everton viral stat. He might well retire as one of the best-ever players to never win anything.

This isn’t to suggest Pickford has been a liability for England. He’s earned his cult-hero status, been a dependable international goalkeeper and has never explicitly let his country down on the biggest stage.

But there is a pattern of smaller disappointments. Mikkel Damsgaard’s free-kick at Euro 2020, Andreas Schjelderup at the World Cup and Enzo Fernandez in the semi-final were all efforts a truly world-class shot-stopper might’ve saved.

There are also questions about his mentality in possession. When the pressure rises, Pickford’s instinct is often to go long rather than help England play through it. That makes sense, given he’s spent the vast majority of his club career at a backs-against-the-wall Everton side.

Tuchel faced plenty of criticism for allowing England to retreat so deeply against Argentina, and rightly so by leaning into it with conservative substitutions. But the manager was only responding to what was happening on the pitch – and Pickford was arguably the most responsible for inviting wave after wave of attack.

Rather than play short and give England a chance to build attacks, he repeatedly launched the ball into the channels, surrendering possession and inviting Argentina straight back onto them. Their equaliser came just 56 seconds after one such clearance.

Admittedly, the final half-hour against Spain followed a similar pattern, and Trafford’s long-distance kicking left a lot to be desired. But he’s at least theoretically equipped to play out from the back, having worked under Pep Guardiola and now being asked to do exactly that at Daniel Farke’s Leeds. He did so adeptly when Tuchel’s Three Lions were well on top for over an hour until the red card.

More importantly, when England came under siege, he produced the spectacular match-winning saves that Pickford hadn’t against Argentina. His miraculous last-gasp double-save secured the Player of the Match award and vindicated Tuchel’s decision to give him his big chance.

A look back at some of James Trafford’s saves from last night 🔥 pic.twitter.com/BLEMO1YAsD

— ITV Football (@itvfootball) November 16, 2026

The situation is beginning to resemble Arsenal’s signing of David Raya, when Mikel Arteta awkwardly but diplomatically insisted there was still a genuine battle for the spot between the sticks. It quickly became apparent that Aaron Ramsdale, for all his honesty, application and work ethic, had been upgraded upon.

We might see the charade continue for a little while, with the two goalkeepers rotated, but the evidence is increasingly difficult to ignore. Tuchel has a new first-choice, and that much ought to be clear by the time that Euro 2028 rolls around.

In another life, Trafford is nursing a pint of Taddy Lager in the corner of a Sam Smith’s, chatting about music and asking how your degree is going. In this one, he’s England’s No.1.

#1426. Euro 2028 Power Rankings: Every major nation ranked from worst to best – England where?

UEFA Euro 2028 is the next major tournament on the horizon for European teams, but who is currently looking like the favourite to win it?

With the tournament still two years away, there is plenty of time for the pecking order to change, but some nations are already looking stronger than others.

The next edition of the European tournament is to be hosted in the UK and Ireland after their joint bid went unopposed, and here’s who we fancy for the tournament at this stage.

Home advantage may help, but this is just not a very good Irish squad.

They are in the second tier of the Nations League but have won just one of their five games and are somehow behind Kosovo in the standings.

Caoimhin Kelleher is probably the most talented member of the squad, while Premier League players Nathan Collins, Jake O’Brien and Dara O’Shea try to protect him, but they are really lacking up front.

Swansea’s Adam Idah is starting alongside Troy Parrott, and the team have managed just six goals in their five games.

Scotland at least made it to the World Cup but stuck the place out.

That cost Steve Clarke his job, and the Scottish FA went bold with their choice of Sebastien Pocognoli, just the second foreign manager to take charge.

Results have been mixed so far, with two wins, one draw and two defeats in their Nations League campaign, and the problem has often been scoring goals. Scott McTominay is deployed as a forward, demonstrating the lack of better options.

At the moment, the country’s best-ever player, Robert Lewandowski, looks likely to continue playing until 2028 but, regardless of how good he was, he will be 39, verging on 40, come the tournament.

His athleticism will undoubtedly have dropped, but you don’t lose that kind of goalscoring ability, and so if you can make a system that gets the ball to him, he can be effective.

To do that, head coach Jan Urban deploys a 4-4-2 with Karol Swiderski alongside him, but it has resulted in mixed success. Poland are third in Nations League B Group 4.

Be careful choosing Turkiye as your dark horses, for they are not the team they once were.

They are currently bottom of Group 1 in Nations League A after losing all six of the games they have played, shipping 15 goals in that time.

They have scored four in that time, one of which was an incredible free kick from Arda Guler, who is clearly the star of the team.

Another couple of seasons playing for Madrid and he will likely have developed into an even better player, but he does not have a huge amount of quality around him. Can Uzun and Brighton’s Ferdi Kadioglu are the other rated players in a largely mediocre squad.

Their biggest challenge will be keeping hold of Craig Bellamy, who has now been scouted for jobs at Burnley and West Ham. The former Cardiff City midfielder has returned the country to form after a really fallow period.

The team is full of familiar Premier League faces such as Harry Wilson, Brennan Johnson, Dan James and Ethan Ampadu, while there are hopes Liverpool’s Lewis Koumas can develop into a top-level striker.

The fact that it is at home makes Wales a contender, but it is hard to see them repeating their 2016 performance.

The 2004 winners have recovered from their awful run that had them as low as 60th in the FIFA rankings at one point and are currently second in a Nations League group that features the Netherlands and Germany.

They really don’t score much, with Arsenal’s Tzolis being one of five players to have a single goal to their name, and they can ship a fair few too, having lost 7-0 to the Dutch.

But putting that one bad night at the office to one side, Greece are a competitive international outfit once again.

The best days may be behind them, but the next generation of Croatian talent is more than capable.

Their strength is in defence, with the Premier League’s Josko Gvardiol and Luka Vuskovic playing alongside each other, while Mateo Kovacic is in midfield.

But there are some other areas where the squad is undeniably old. Ivan Perisic and Luka Modric are both still starting, and the country lacks a top-level striker.

Sweden are the latest country to find that two of their best talents naturally play in the same position, but they are so far making it work with a 4-4-2 system under Graham Potter.

Alexander Isak has been a little slow going, with just one goal in the Nations League this season, but the same cannot be said for Viktor Gyokeres, who looks a different player in the Sweden shirt than he does in the Arsenal one.

He’s got six goals in the Nations League as Sweden top their group, having failed to win just one match.

Behind the strikers, it becomes a little more suspect, with Brighton’s Yasin Ayari and Newcastle’s Anthony Elanga ahead of Victor Lindelof, but it is a decent team.

Ralf Rangnick has been leading an Austrian revolution, and they could have gone further in the summer’s World Cup had the draw been a little kinder. After managing to come second in a group that featured Argentina, Austria faced eventual champions Spain and unsurprisingly lost.

Rangnick has instilled a pressing philosophy into the team while keeping them very solid at the back too. No team has scored more goals in Nations League B, while only Northern Ireland have a better defensive record.

Rasmus Hojlund has proven to be far more effective for his country than he ever was for Manchester United. The striker has scored five goals in Denmark’s Nations League campaign, and he, alongside Mikkel Damsgaard and Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg, are the names you are likely to be most familiar with.

They are good at scoring too, currently averaging the fourth-highest number of goals per game in Nations League A.

The eternal dark horses are currently demolishing their Nations League group, with just one goal conceded in five games and four wins. Granted, it is a group made up of Slovenia, Scotland and North Macedonia.

But Switzerland often do well in international tournaments. They reached the World Cup quarter-finals, losing to eventual finalists Argentina, and in the previous Euros, they lost to eventual finalists England again in the quarter-finals.

Squad-wise, John Manzambi is the star in a team largely without one.

Italy are god-awful when it comes to qualifying for a tournament, but when they do get there, they often do very well.

It is not the strongest Italian generation by any stretch. Premier League stars Sandro Tonali and Riccardo Calafiori lead the way, but Inter’s Francesco Pio Esposito has got five goals in his country’s Nations League campaign.

Alessandro Bastoni and Nicolo Barella are experienced members of the squad, while Gianluigi Donnarumma is a good keeper, even if he can sometimes throw in a goal.

Roberto Mancini knows what he’s doing, having guided Italy to Euro 2020 success in England, but you would still have to put them down as outsiders.

READ: 7 forgotten ballers you won’t believe are still playing international football

This generation’s Iceland are stronger than their Viking relatives, not least because they have one of the best strikers in the world.

It is not a case of Haaland + everyone else, though. Martin Odegaard performs particularly well for his country, while Antonio Nusa and Oscar Bobb are good options on the wing.

Defensively, they are a little short, but if they can score enough, keeping clean sheets doesn’t really matter.

Kevin De Bruyne is the last remnant of Belgium’s golden generation that never really shone, but the next generation is proving itself capable enough.

Atalanta’s Charles De Ketelaere has chipped in with a goal and four assists, but it is De Bruyne who still provides the main threat.

Belgium’s current position in world football is perhaps best demonstrated by the fact that they have beaten both Italy and Turkey twice in their Nations League group but lost both games to France, one of which was 4-1.

Successive poor tournament performances meant Germany needed a fun injection, and so they hired the man with the biggest smile in world football. Unfortunately for Jurgen Klopp, it is a pretty average crop of Germany players.

Klopp wants to get the best out of Florian Wirtz because the options behind him are even worse, while Kai Havertz will not go down as one of the best German strikers of all time.

Defence is okay, with Malick Thiaw and Nico Schlotterbeck, but two wins, two draws and a defeat in Klopp’s first five games give an indication of the talent level of the squad.

It’s not Van Persie and Robben levels of talent, but this is a very good crop of Dutch players.

Premier League regulars Jurrien Timber, Cody Gakpo, Micky van de Ven and Jan Paul van Hecke make up the core of the outfield, while Barcelona’s Frenkie De Jong has the armband.

Donyell Malen is the number nine, and you could say the lack of an elite striker is a concern, but they did just stuff seven past Greece.

They are led by Xavi, and you do not need too many attempts to guess what kind of football the Cruyff disciple plays.

It is working too, with the country having the second-best goals-per-match and goals-conceded-per-match records in the Nations League top flight.

They have often been the nearly men of tournaments and certainly have the talent to be so again, while they hope for more.

Portugal are finally free of the existential crisis of Cristiano Ronaldo, and so the focus can finally be on the other players in the squad.

The Iberian team boast probably the best midfield in world football, with Vitinha and Joao Neves guiding PSG to back-to-back Champions League titles. Behind them, Mateus Fernandes continues to improve.

Rafa Leao took Ronaldo’s number seven shirt, but Goncalo Ramos has often performed well when given a chance.

Bruno Fernandes will turn 34 during the tournament but has yet to experience a huge drop-off, even if he has been a little off it this season.

Defence-wise, Ruben Dias is the starting centre-back in an area that is easily the weakest of the team.

There’s regime change in Paris, with Zinedine Zidane taking over from Didier Deschamps, but the bar has been set very high.

France have been the most consistent national team of the last 15 years. Quarter-finalists in the 2014 World Cup, they became winners in 2018 and runners-up in 2022. A fourth-place finish at the 2026 World Cup was seen as a failure. That’s how high the standard is.

In the Euros, France finished second to surprise winners Portugal in 2016 before being knocked out in the round of 16 in 2020. A semi-final in Euro 2024 was a return to form.

Zidane’s biggest problem is how to get all of his many attacking stars on the pitch at the same time.

Michael Olise, Kylian Mbappe, Desire Doue, Bradley Barcola, Rayan Cherki and Ousmane Dembele would all start for any other national team. The emergence of Eli Junior Kroupi is another card for Zidane to work out when to play.

If you were picking holes in the team, you may isolate midfield as one of the weaker areas. Adrien Rabiot and Lucas Da Cunha are not Paul Pogba and N’Golo Kante.

Defence is strong, though, with Ibrahim Konate and Jeremy Jacquet filling in until William Saliba returns to full fitness.

Balancing attack versus defence was what Zidane did well at Madrid, so you would back him to do the same in the job he waited so long for.

England are pretty bloody good when it comes to home tournaments.

Three FIFA/UEFA tournaments have been hosted in the UK, and the worst England have done in them is third place.

They won the World Cup back in 1966, which, yes, we will still talk about, thank you, and even spectacular failure in Euro 96 resulted in third place. In Euro 2020, which was spread across the continent, England played all but one game at Wembley as they reached the final.

Spectacular failure came into effect once again as they lost on penalties, which is about as English as getting sand in your chips on a seaside holiday.

England already know that, should they qualify, all of their group games will be at Wembley. Win the group and they will have one game away from London in Newcastle before exclusively playing at their home stadium until the end of the tournament.

The odds, then, are very much in England’s favour, but 68 years of hurt have taught every England fan to be wary of getting their hopes up.

In terms of the squad, it is the best tournament team for generations, having reached the last two Euros finals. They can also boast some of the best young talent in the world, with Jude Bellingham showing a particular tendency to perform for his country on the big stages.

Harry Kane will turn 35 during the tournament but has the technical quality to still be an asset at that age. The win over Spain feels like the kind of statement a team needs.

There are question marks over Thomas Tuchel, with the scar of the Argentina semi-final still raw, but he is one of the best managers in the world. England should fancy their chances.

A loss at home to England should be seen as a mere speed bump on what has otherwise been Spain’s all-conquering run to the top of world football.

They are reigning World and European champions, and their squad is stacked with talent.

Lamine Yamal is the headline grabber, although he was largely anonymous in the summer’s World Cup, but there are high-level players all over the squad. Pau Cubarsi is emerging as one of the world’s best defenders, while Fermin Lopez is having an excellent season with Barcelona.

In midfield, Rodri, Pedri, Fabian Ruiz and plenty more can keep the ball for fun, and when David Raya is your second-choice keeper, you know something is going well.

Spain could lose every game from now until the start of the tournament, and they should still be considered favourites.

#1424. Pat Cummins' remarkable 68-minute press conference took a clear-eyed and devastating aim at Usman Khawaja's integrity - Australia are in a civil war with no obvious resolution, writes LAWRENCE BOOTH

Published: 05:20 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 05:21 EST, 13 November 2026

Pat Cummins is either the greatest actor in world sport – or the claim that the whole Australian team knew about the sandpaper plot in South Africa eight years ago is a figment of Usman Khawaja’s imagination.

After Cummins’s remarkable press conference in Sydney on Friday morning, in which he called Khawaja’s various assertions ‘complete and utter nonsense’ and questioned the validity of their friendship, it was hard to discern any common ground, much less spot a middle way.

According to the blue corner, everyone was in on the scam, sandpaper was used not just at Cape Town but in the previous Test at Port Elizabeth, and there was a team meeting to discuss the question of collective responsibility.

According to the red, those who knew about the plan did not include the bowlers, nothing untoward happened at Port Elizabeth, and there was no meeting.

The only thing that can be said for certain after another tumultuous 24 hours for Australian cricket was that the two corners are now polar opposites, each eyeing the other with suspicion and incredulity. Barring an improbable climbdown, the twain can never meet.

Cummins, it must be said, eased into his work after an emotional start behind a lectern at the Cricket Central venue in Sydney’s Olympic Park. He began by stating his basic position, then invited questions, which for the next hour and a bit he handled with aplomb and a degree of statesmanship.

Pat Cummins held a remarkable press conference in Sydney to address the sandpaper claims

Speaking for more than an hour, Cummins dismissed Khawaja’s various assertions as ‘complete and utter nonsense’ and questioned the validity of their friendship

This will not please those who still find it impossible to believe that Cummins and his fellow seamers on that trip, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc, knew nothing of the scheme that led to bans for three batsmen – Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

After all, as any bowler will tell you, the idea that the condition of their most prized possession might be altered without their noticing is as absurd as trying to persuade a batsman to walk out without his favourite willow.

And yet. Cummins stuck to his guns, in contrast to Khawaja’s appearance on the ABC on Wednesday evening, when he repeatedly declined to name Cummins as one of the guilty party. And while Khawaja reacted to his TV grilling by cancelling media engagements, Cummins made it clear he would be answering every question that came his way.

Whichever side you believe, and whatever the doubts that remain, his press conference grabbed the momentum from Team Khawaja.

It also made the previous day’s appearance by Mitchell Marsh, Australia’s white-ball captain for the next three weeks against England, all the more bizarre. By refusing to engage with any of the questions raised by Khawaja’s autobiography, Marsh – himself a veteran of South Africa 2018 – did little to dispel the suspicion that Khawaja had a point.

And that in turn encouraged the view that Cummins, who called his own press conference without the knowledge of Cricket Australia, might be about to come clean.

Instead, he doubled down on the denial he and his bowling colleagues had issued in 2021, but now went further, taking a clear-eyed and devastating aim at Khawaja’s integrity.

‘Usman is a friend, but friends aren’t casual with each other’s lives and reputations,’ said Cummins. ‘He’s dealt with the way he’s presented his story in a very casual manner and it affects a lot of people. That’s what I’m grappling with at the moment, because I don’t think that’s OK. It’s not what friends do.’

Cummins plainly intended this to be his final word on the matter, but the problem facing Australian cricket is that the sore may never properly heal.

David Warner then hit back at Cummins and accused him of 'throwing Khawaja under the bus'

Only a couple of hours after Cummins finished, Warner – at Perth’s Optus Stadium as a TV pundit for the first ODI between Australia and England – was being asked for his view, and he didn’t hold back, repeating his belief that Khawaja’s version of events was ‘the truth’.

He added: ‘I really, really support him. I actually feel for him at the moment. I feel that the captain today threw Uzzy under the bus and I’m very, very disappointed about that.’

Disappointment. It’s mutual, and it’s everywhere. Cummins provided a brief distraction, but it doesn’t change the fact that this is a civil war with no obvious resolution.

Offered the chance to kick Australian cricket while it was down, England made humiliating contact with fresh air on the opening day of their eight-match white-ball trip.

Only hours after Pat Cummins had added a twist to the sandpaper saga by dismissing Usman Khawaja’s claims that the whole squad knew about the ball-tampering plans in South Africa eight years ago as ‘complete and utter nonsense’, Harry Brook’s side were blown away for 131 in the first ODI – having at one stage been 65 for eight.

Australia then romped home by seven wickets with more than 26 overs in hand to take a 1–0 lead into the second game of this three-match series in Adelaide on Sunday. For England, anyway, complete and utter nonsense felt about right.

It is not quite a year since they began their Ashes campaign here at the Optus Stadium by being bowled out in 32.5 overs in their first innings and 34.4 in their second – before stumbling to a 4–1 defeat.

Now, they obligingly split the difference, dismissed in 33.4 as Mahli Beardman, a 21-year-old fast bowler from Dunsborough, a couple of hours drive down the coast from Perth, picked up six for 34 – the best figures for Australia by an ODI debutant.

His first victim was Joe Root, caught behind for a painful 17 off 36 balls, and his second Brook, who had made only a single when he fidgeted fatally outside off stump.

That might have been enough to satisfy most newcomers, but Beardman had barely started. Jordan Cox made two before edging a poke, and Sam Curran top-edged a pull to fine leg for a duck.

When Liam Dawson, yet to score, squeezed a drive to backward point, Beardman had five wickets in 28 balls – not bad for a player whose only previous taste of international cricket had come in a T20 in Pakistan in January.

He then ended a lively last-wicket stand of 29 by removing Jofra Archer, who had just driven him down the ground for four. It was the only authentic boundary England managed off his bowling: the other, a streaky inside edge from Root, summed up the problems posed by his pace, bounce and accuracy. As bids for a place on next summer’s Ashes tour go, this was hard to ignore.

‘Laying in bed last night, that’s not what I had planned,’ said Beardman, who was taken under his wing by Australian fast-bowling legend Dennis Lillee after a mutual friend spotted him as a young teenager bowling at a bin down the side of a house. ‘It was an incredible game and it all happened so fast.’

If England had learned lessons from their collapses in the last year’s Test here, they showed little sign of being able to implement them. Players drove on the up, as they had so heedlessly a year earlier, and failed to cope with the Perth bounce.

England head coach Brendon McCullum was critical of his side's failure to adapt to the pitch, and called on them to learn from their mistakes going forward.

'It’s a bit like batting on a trampoline,' said McCullum. 'There are certain shots that are very difficult to execute. We talked about trying to put those away. We probably knew we were in for a low-scoring contest, but we expected to get a few more runs than 130.

'We're disappointed but there are some good lessons for us. If you look towards the World Cup in South Africa there’s going to be some pitches there that will test us from a bounce point of view.'

And all this after they had played a warm-up game at the WACA – a grievous omission before the Ashes – and trained with such intensity that white-ball mentor Kevin Pietersen had declared it the best practice session he had seen from an England team.

In the event, their top-scorer was Gus Atkinson, who hit an unbeaten 29 from No 10, including England’s only six.

Mitchell Marsh, stroke-less in the previous day’s press conference, put that into perspective by clearing the ropes four times during a 29-ball half-century, while Cooper Connolly – dropped by Tom Banton at midwicket on five – hit two sixes himself.

England’s only consolation had come at the start of Australia’s reply, when Atkinson bowled Travis Head first ball off the inside edge. Head it was who had taken care of Australia’s fourth-innings chase here a year ago, thrashing a 69-ball century that knocked the stuffing out of Ben Stokes’s attack.

Instead, it was Marsh who went for his shots, stopped only when he flicked Jamie Overton to Ben Duckett at deep midwicket, by which time Australia were already halfway there. For a few hours, at least, no one was talking about sandpaper.

#1422. Next USA manager: 7 options to replace Pochettino after Man Utd hire

Mauricio Pochettino is preparing for his USA farewell as he gets set to start his Manchester United reign. But who’s going to step into his shoes next?

US Soccer have already dreamt about Pep Guardiola becoming the next manager of their men’s national team, but the latest reports say the answer will be a thanks, but no thanks.

Who else could they turn to, then? Pochettino could be a tough act to follow, after all, even if he didn’t get them as far in the World Cup as they’d have liked.

They’ll be losing a high-profile coach capable of generating international attention and now have a void to fill.

Here are some potential contenders for the USMNT job.

Not as big a name internationally as Pochettino, sure, but Cherundolo might be the obvious option from within.

A former right-back who earned more than 80 caps for the USA, he took charge of their under-23 national team earlier this year in view of the 2028 Olympics.

The former Las Vegas Lights and Los Angeles FC coach will also serve as interim manager of the senior side after Pochettino’s exit.

Could he get the permanent job? It might depend on how the interview process goes with other candidates. Pochettino will still oversee the last USA fixture of the November international break and you’d imagine they’d want to have a permanent successor chosen before the next one in March.

But Cherundolo, 47, might have some backers as someone who knows the system.

At this stage, it seems unlikely Southgate will return to management after leaving the England job in 2024.

“Towards the end of my time with England, I stopped enjoying the wins that keep you going. By the end, I didn’t enjoy the wins for any longer than a couple of minutes,” he said earlier this year, before adding: “My desire to be involved in football has changed.”

Fair enough if that’s what you want, Sir Gareth, but we think it’d be a shame for him to leave management behind completely.

Going back into club football doesn’t interest him at all, but could a different international job in an English-speaking country? Who knows.

The USA job might be the kind of project that would have floated his boat when his hunger for management was bigger. There’s an appetite to build something there and Southgate knows what it takes to go far in tournaments, even if he wasn’t quite the man to get England over the line.

We equally think it’d be a shame if the last sight of Bielsa as a manager was his early exit from the World Cup with a drab Uruguay side.

At 71, he has every right to put his feet up and reflect on an influential career. But is there room for a more fitting end?

Bielsa has plenty of experience managing at international level. He’s had spells with Argentina, Chile and Uruguay, but it’s fair to say some of his better work was in the club game.

A meticulous coach if ever there was one, Bielsa showed at Leeds United his capability for building a project from the ground up and getting almost universal buy-in.

He even once managed a club called America. If that isn’t a sign…

Perhaps a more realistic contender from the pool of managers last employed by a country instead of a club, Martinez resigned from the Portugal job after the World Cup.

It’s been a decade since he started out in international management with Belgium. Judging his time there is a bit tricky. Did he underachieve with the talent at his disposal? Probably. Did he still do pretty well at some tournaments? You could say so.

But to protect his reputation, he needed to do a better job with Portugal than he eventually managed.

Now Martinez faces having to rebuild his managerial career. Doing so outside of Europe entirely might be what he needs.

It’d be a risky choice for the USA but it’s not an unimaginable one.

From the current crop of MLS managers, the most likely to become a candidate for the USMNT job is probably Callaghan.

Currently in charge of Nashville SC, he was the USA’s interim manager in 2023, in between Gregg Berhalter’s spells at the helm.

Callaghan had been an assistant to Berhalter but has since forged his own path in coaching, taking charge of Nashville in 2024.

There was a brief time when it felt like Nagelsmann might be a rival to Pochettino for the Man Utd job. What if he replaced him for the USA instead?

Once one of the Bundesliga’s most promising young coaches, he turned his hand to international management for a three-year spell in charge of Germany.

But he’s been out of work since leaving that role in the summer and needs to find the next step.

Nagelsmann can communicate in English and has shown serious potential from the touchline before. His next move will be crucial and he’ll have to weigh up whether to stay in the international game or go back to club football, but he could bring some innovative ideas.

It’s doubtful if Henry will ever return to management, but he hasn’t ruled it out.

He last held a management role in 2024, leading France at the Olympics and somehow managing not to win gold.

Henry is a familiar face to American soccer fans. He used to play for New York Red Bulls, once managed Montreal Impact and is a regular pundit on CBS Sports.

He’s suggested a willingness to take charge of the USMNT before, saying a couple of years ago: “Do I know the players? Yeah, I know the players. Do I know the league? Yeah, I know the league. It’s a different ballgame, I cannot talk about it now like that, but would I want to be a manager at any level? Yes, of course. That’s one of the things I’d like to do.”

Come to think of it, this one could actually tick a few boxes. But it’d be a bit of a gamble in the first place.

#1421. Why Man United staff feel treatment of Michael Carrick was 'disgusting' and the comment from Omar Berrada that raised eyebrows as club legend is put out of his misery - and Mauricio Pochettino gets set to take over

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER and DANIEL MATTHEWS, US SENIOR SPORTS WRITER

Published: 14:25 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 07:15 EST, 13 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino would have been fast asleep in his hotel room in the quirky American town of Trilith when Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox sat down with Michael Carrick at Carrington Thursday morning and confirmed the worst-kept secret in football.

It was time for Carrick to vacate the head coach’s office at Manchester United, and safe to say Pochettino will have his feet under the desk this time next week.

Carrick arrived at 7.50am but, unlike the last two days, he was no longer wearing his United training gear.

The agonising wait to be put out of his misery was over, and the club’s chief executive and director of football duly administered the last rites before Carrick left at 10.18am.

The decision was communicated to staff and Under-21s boss Adam Lawrence took training with the players who have remained at Carrington during the international break.

The first reports of Carrick’s sacking broke at 9.30am, but United insisted that they were premature and it wasn’t until 10.37am that the news was confirmed in a 142-word statement.

Michael Carrick finally left Carrington on Thursday morning after an agonising wait to be put out of his misery

Staff at Manchester United believe that the former club captain's treatment at the hands of their Ineos paymasters has been 'disgusting'

It's understood that his backroom staff - assistant Steve Holland, coaches Jonathan Woodgate, Jonny Evans and Travis Binnion, and goalkeeper coach Craig Mawson - have also gone. When Evans left on Wednesday night with his car piled high with cardboard boxes, it didn't bode well.

The treatment of Carrick and Evans, in particular, has upset staff. Two highly-respected figures at United, whose association with the club goes back more than 20 years, have been left hanging while their employers stumble over a succession plan.

Members of staff share Gary Neville’s view that Berrada and Wilcox meeting with Sir Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco, and making a move for Pochettino while Carrick had to keep driving past the cameras on his way into Carrington for the last three days, was ‘disgusting’.

It has also reignited anger over the 450 job cuts carried out by Ratcliffe and Ineos over the past three years while pouring millions down the drain in compensation.

The £10million to buy Pochettino and his staff out of their contracts with the US Soccer Federation, and the pay-off owing to Carrick and Co, will push the cost of hiring and firing coaches in the Ineos era close to £50m.

No wonder eyebrows were raised when Berrada spoke at Sir Alex Ferguson’s 40th anniversary dinner at Old Trafford on Friday night and talked about building a culture at the club.

The feeling is that changing United’s head coach won’t make a shred of difference if there isn’t significant change higher up the chain.

It has once again turned the spotlight on the relationship between Ratcliffe and the Glazer family, who from February can force him to sell his 28 per cent holding to a third party for less than the £25-per-share he paid in 2024 unless he can match the offer and buy the club himself.

However, United sources say they had little choice but to sack Carrick with the club in the relegation zone, having decided to give him a stay of execution at the end of last month.

Since then, the club had carried out a comprehensive review and come to the conclusion that a record of one win from 10 Premier League games was unacceptable.

The sources indicated that the United board shared the frustration and anger felt by fans over the situation, and believe that a change of head coach will bring about an improvement from a squad that is far better than results would suggest.

While United praised Carrick for his ‘highest degree of professionalism’, there was only silence from the players on social media.

Many of them are on international duty, including Bruno Fernandes whose criticism of Carrick’s tactics after the Champions League defeat to Como proved so damaging.

Following the announcement of Carrick's dismissal none of his former players - including Bruno Fernandes - were quick to say their goodbyes publicly

Meanwhile, his would-be successor Mauricio Pochettino is set to face the media on Friday

Pochettino will inherit this squad of players once he has completed his duties as US national team coach with the upcoming CONCACAF Nations League double-header against Haiti.

The former Tottenham and Chelsea boss is due to speak at 2.15pm Friday ahead of the first leg in Miami on Saturday night when he will face questions over the United job for the first time.

Pochettino is expected to stay in charge for the second leg in Cincinnati in the early hours of Wednesday morning before flying to Manchester to meet the players and prepare for the crunch clash with Liverpool at Anfield a week on Sunday.

The US have been staying in Trilith, near their new training headquarters in Fayetteville south-west of Atlanta, where they were also based before the World Cup.

It’s a unique place designed for the film industry and built around the Trilith Studios which are the largest outside Hollywood. The ideal place for Pochettino to prepare for life at Old Trafford.

He has embraced the American lifestyle since he was appointed US coach in September 2024, a few months after leaving Chelsea, and will be sorry to leave.

Pochettino is said to have developed a love of bourbon whiskey, country music and Nashville, with Ella Langley’s Choosin’ Texas one of his favourite tunes.

He has admitted crying over Miracle, the movie about the US hockey team made up of college kids famously beating the Soviet Union to the gold medal at the 1980 Winter Olympics.

But the pull of Manchester United was always going to be too great, and very soon he will be swapping Trilith for Old Trafford.

France star Desire Doue was left with a loose front tooth after being hit with a nasty elbow in France's 3-1 defeat to Italy in the Nations League.

The PSG winger was left in need of some emergency dental work by Italy's Davide Frattesi who caught the 21-year-old in the mouth while shielding the ball.

In his post match interview French boss Zinedine Zidane, when asked if Doue had lost a tooth, replied: 'Yeah I think so. We’re going to take him straight there, a tooth has come loose I think, we’ll take care of him starting tomorrow.'

It was a poor day all round for the Frenchman who not only had his tooth dislodged but was also unable to impact a poor game for Les Blues in which the Azzuri beat them at the San Siro.

To compound Doue's misery it was the offender Frattesi who scored Italy's second goal in the 3-1 win just six minutes before he performed some unorthodox dentistry.

The Lazio midfielder's goal completed the Italians' comeback after going 1-0 down to a Michael Olise goal just ten minutes in before Inter Milan's Francesco Esposito levelled things up just 16 minutes later.

Desire Doue was left with a loose front tooth after receiving an elbow in the mouth from Davide Fratessi

Fratessi got away with just a yellow card as Italy beat the French 3-1 at the San Siro

Frattesi gave Italy the lead early on in the second half before Esposito netted his second from the spot to put the game out of reach.

Speaking after the game Zidane was surprisingly positive about his team's performance despite the loss, saying that losing is, 'part of the process.'

The French then went onto say: 'The most important thing is creating chances. Hitting the post had an impact, but I'm not disappointed.

'I would have been if we hadn't created good possession. What we need to analyse is why we weren't at the right level off the ball.'

The World Cup winner was not entirely positive however, later saying: 'in the second half we ran into difficulties, especially defensively.'

The victory put Italy level on points with the French in Group A with both sides having won three drawn one and lost one.

But France will have an opportunity to right their wrongs and return to the top of the group on Sunday as they welcome Turkey.

But if Italy beat Belgium on the same day the French will have to settle for second.

#1418. Why England were unremarkable on Harry Kane's big night, the Ben White problem - and established star whose place could be under threat from Morgan Rogers, writes IAN LADYMAN

Published: 02:00 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 07:49 EST, 13 November 2026

England will head to Spain on Sunday for a Nations League shoot out with the World Champions. A win in Madrid could see Thomas Tuchel's team progress to the quarter-finals next March as group winners.

It wasn't always easy on Harry Kane's big night at Wembley against Croatia, though. Indeed this was probably England's worst performance since losing to Argentina in the World Cup semi-final last July.

Here Daily Mail Sport looks at the key issues emerging from last night's tight squeeze.

Self-defeating abuse of White is madness and must stop

In case nobody has noticed, England are not over stocked with competent right-backs.

Trent Alexander-Arnold isn't wholly trusted in big games by Thomas Tuchel, Reece James is always injured and Tino Livramento has also struggled to be available. Why, then, is a significant section of the England support so determined to drive Ben White away from the international scene?

White plays for Arsenal, the champions of England. He is a fine, versatile defender who would be gratefully received and appreciated by fans of most national teams in world football. He had issues with the previous England management regime and does not apologise for that.

Ben White was booed when he came on. The abuse towards the defender must stop

He spoke about it this week and made it clear he didn't wish to reopen old wounds. All that matters now is that he is willing and available. But – despite a plea from Tuchel before this game – England fans still booed him when he came on as a substitute last night.

It's a disgraceful way to treat a footballer who can be an asset to his country going forwards and it's something the England manager cares deeply about. Do we want to win the next Euros or not? Do we want our best players motivated and driven and part of the squad? Or do we want to faff about harbouring old grudges related to a situation in Qatar four winters ago that none of us really know that much about?

The choice is clear. If we are not careful, we will drive a good footballer away from the England set-up for good. It's madness.

Big night for Kane but questions for England

They came to celebrate Harry Kane and the England captain got his goal. Number 92 for the striker. Beneath all the fuss over England's talisman, however, this came perilously close to being a step backwards for Thomas Tuchel's England.

The England manager has been saying since the last international break in September and October that he wanted his team to go to Madrid on Sunday in with a shout at knocking Spain from the top of this Nations League Group. Had Croatia been a little smarter in front of goal at Wembley last night, England would have been heading for a dead rubber against the world champions.

Harry Kane scored on his big night as England edged out a 2-1 win over Croatia at Wembley

It was a night to remember for Kane as he was honoured after receiving his record 126th cap

Three times in the last ten minutes of this game, Croatia had good opportunities to score a second goal and take a point from the game that would have been perfectly justified. So England crawled over the line but there was little here that was impressive with questions emerging once again about how capable really are when they don't have the ball.

Kane put it well himself afterwards when he said: 'You can't always expect things to be perfect. Of course, we know we can improve on a few bits and we will need to if we want to win on Sunday.'

Tuchel himself will perhaps have quiet concerns. One of the German's worries about this England team is that they sometimes struggle to take training performances on to the field and this was another case in point.

The ultimate target for this team is to win the home Euros in 2028 and the pressure will need handling in front of their own supporters if they are to do that. With that in mind, it's good to know that the FA are interested in hosting the finals of this Nations League competition next summer.

If England make it through next March's two-legged quarter-finals, they could do with some practice of playing high-stakes games at Wembley.

Asked last week on the day he announced his squad whether Jordan Pickford was still his number one goalkeeper, Tuchel was unequivocal.

'He is,' said Tuchel. 'But the competition is on there as well. Like for the outfield players. And James Trafford will get regular starts now, that's what we wanted. They shared the matches last time. There's an opportunity that we maybe do this again.'

Morgan Rogers impressed after opening the scoring inside the opening half-an-hour

Jordan Pickford starting against Croatia could lead to James Trafford playing against Spain

With all this in mind, it was expected that Trafford would start this game with Pickford getting the gloves for the one that really matters in Spain on Sunday. That wasn't the case, so we wait with interest to see what the England manager does in Madrid.

What nobody really wants is for a return to the situation we had in the 1980s when Ron Greenwood used to rotate between the late Ray Clemence and last night's guest of honour Peter Shilton.

England's back four is the one area of this team that can look unconvincing – they did again last night - and the last thing they need is not to know who their goalkeeper is from one match to the next. Tuchel is going to have to make a decision.

Interesting that Tuchel chose to put Dan Burn into his team for this game, despite the Newcastle defender not being in the original squad.

With Marc Guehi and Ezri Konsa both absent with injuries, Everton's Jarrod Branthwaite would have expected to play on the left of Jarell Quansah here. Instead, Burn leapfrogged him in the queue and maybe we should have paid more attention to something Tuchel said the day before the game.

'Jarrad Branthwaite is doing very well but it's a very different style of play for him from Everton towards us,' said Tuchel.

Jarrad Branthwaite clearly has a way to go before he's fully trusted to start by Thomas Tuchel

'You can see that Dan Burn is straight away a big voice in training and is more used to the style with Newcastle from the last two seasons with Eddie Howe where they followed in a high press and to man-man. And of course he was with us at the World Cup so he is used a bit more to our style of play.'

That's all very well and logical but – that being the case – why was Branthwaite chosen ahead of Burn in the original group of 25 last Friday? Burn, as it happened, had a very good game last night.

Tuchel talks always about the value of players being in camp. 'The train is leaving the station,' is one of the England manager's more memorable quotes of recent times. Players like Cole Palmer, for example, have learned to their cost that missing meet-ups with injuries can be costly.

Bukayo Saka is not in that category and has plenty of credit in the bank with the England manager. However, Tuchel's fondness for Morgan Rogers is well known and Saka's absence does give him a way of getting the Chelsea player into his team. Rogers may be a number ten at heart but he was effective once again here out on the right side.

The 24-year-old was one of England's better players on a muted night against Croatia and he deserved his first half goal. He gives England a more direct, athletic dimension on the opposite flank to the more balletic offerings of Anthony Gordon. Food for thought for Tuchel at least as Saka continues his own battle against persistent injuries.

Bukayo Saka's long-term place in England's team could be under threat from Morgan Rogers

Newcastle United were pretty much an open door in the summer as they sold players left right and centre. Gordon to Barcelona to make sure the club was the right side of the financial guidelines and then Sandro Tonali to Tottenham and Bruno Guimaraes to Arsenal simply because the players made it known they wanted to go.

Strange, then, that Manchester United didn't make a proper move for left-back Lewis Hall. Admittedly this wasn't the most difficult match in which he will have ever played, but Hall was impressive once again.

With Luke Shaw so injury prone, Hall pretty much has the left-back berth sewn up for England but it feels as though he now needs to make the next step in his club career. United retain a nominal interest but who knows what incoming manager Mauricio Pochettino may think? It's hard to work out why United didn't try harder to sign him last summer. He has subsequently signed a new contract at Newcastle, of course.

#1417. Mauricio Pochettino is CONFIRMED as new Man United manager: Departing USA boss speaks out as he agrees to succeed Michael Carrick - but faces race against time for first game

Published: 07:02 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 07:51 EST, 13 November 2026

Manchester United have confirmed that Mauricio Pochettino has agreed to become their new head coach on a two-and-a-half-year contract at Old Trafford.

Pochettino will replace Michael Carrick who was sacked following 10 months in charge on Friday, after United agreed to pay more than £10million to buy him and his backroom staff out of their contracts with the US Soccer Federation.

The 54-year-old Argentine will take charge of the USA’s CONCACAF Nations League double-header against Haiti in Miami on Saturday and Cincinnati on Wednesday before beginning his new job as United boss on Wednesday. His first game will be against Liverpool at Anfield a week on Sunday.

There were no comments from Pochettino or United officials in Friday’s press release confirming his appointment because he remains contracted to US Soccer.

Pochettino said in the USMNT's statement: 'The opportunity to represent the USA crest was one of the greatest honors of my career. We are so grateful to the players for their commitment, to the fans for their belief, and to the Federation for always supporting our staff and creating the opportunities to impact the culture of soccer in this great country.'

Pochettino is due to give a pre-match press conference at 2.15pm on Friday, but is not expected to speak about United until he arrives next week.

United sources say that Pochettino’s experience, philosophy, personality and skill-set make him well suited for the job, as well as his record of developing individual talent and building excellent team cultures.

Mauricio Pochettino has been appointed as the Manchester United manager

Michael Carrick was sacked after the club made their worst start to the season in 40 years

A statement from the club read: ‘Mauricio Pochettino has agreed to become the Manchester United men’s head coach from 18 November.

‘The club has reached an agreement with the US Soccer Federation for Mauricio and his staff to be released after the conclusion of their responsibilities with the US men’s national team.

‘The Argentinian is renowned for his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players.

‘Pochettino has consistently performed at the highest level of football across multiple leagues. He began his coaching career with Espanyol in 2009 before joining Southampton and achieving a club-record Premier League points tally in 2014.

‘During five full seasons at Tottenham Hotspur, Pochettino established the club as regular UEFA Champions League contenders, securing qualification in four consecutive seasons and leading the club to its first final in the competition in 2019.

‘In 2021, he joined Paris Saint-Germain, where he won the Ligue 1 title, the Coupe de France and the Trophée des Champions before joining Chelsea in 2023. Most recently he led the U.S. Men’s National Team to the Round of 16 at the FIFA World Cup.’

Earlier in the week, the club's chief executive Omar Berrada and Wilcox flew back from Monaco, where minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe ratified their decision to sack Carrick with the blessing of co-chairmen Joel and Avram Glazer.

Carrick arrived at United's training ground at 7.50am on Thursday morning and was dismissed.

He left at 10.18am, less than two and a half hours later. He became the first Premier League manager to be sacked this season.

United's statement read: 'After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions.

'Michael is, and always will be, a Manchester United legend. Just as he did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club.

'His leadership and achievements last season will always be fondly remembered.'

Sources close to United say the club's leadership believe their squad of players is far better than the performances and results under Carrick indicated.

United feel that the squad are far better than their position in the Premier League shows

They gave the under-fire manager a chance to turn things around against Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa but ultimately felt the team were not on the right path.

It has been a campaign in which United won just three matches, one of which came against Azerbaijani minnows FK Sabah, and they are yet to keep a clean sheet in the league.

Pochettino's United travel to Anfield on November 22 before a Champions League clash at Sporting Lisbon, Pochettino's first home game against Brentford and then away match at Newcastle.
